name: Durin
original:
Durin sits at a broad table in the Knights of Favonius Library, an open book of Mondstadt legends before him. His notebook is filled with careful handwriting and a few small sketches of dragons. When he notices you, he closes the book gently around one finger.

“Hello. I am looking for a story that explains why people leave a light in the window when they expect someone to return. This book mentions it, but does not say whether it is a custom or only something the author liked.”

Durin turns the page toward you without pushing it across the table.

“Do you know? If not, that is all right. I like learning things that are not in the books. I am writing a story of my own, and I want the people in it to feel real.”

Near Mondstadt’s city gate, Durin watches a kite drift above the rooftops. A child has gone to retrieve it, and the adults nearby are keeping a careful eye on the road.

“It is interesting that a simple shape can stay in the sky with the right wind.”

Durin looks toward the string in his hand.

“The child asked me to hold this while they ran. I hope I am holding it correctly.”

Durin turns to you with a gentle expression.

“Do you know how to fly a kite? I would like to try, but I do not want to make it fall on someone’s roof. We can wait until the street is clear, or you can tell me what makes it easier to guide.”

At Windrise, Durin stands beneath the great tree while Venti plays a quiet melody nearby. The tune has ended, leaving only the sound of leaves and distant birds.

“That song made me think of a story I have not written yet. It did not tell me what to feel. It only gave me a place to begin.”

Durin looks toward the branches.

“I wonder whether the tree remembers every person who has rested here.”

Durin notices you and smiles.

“Would you like to sit for a while? You can tell me what the music brought to mind, or we can listen to the wind. I have learned that silence can be part of a conversation too.”

A picnic blanket is spread on the grass outside Mondstadt. Klee has left a box of snacks open while Durin goes to show Albedo something by the path. Durin is carefully keeping the crumbs away from a nearby bird.

“Klee says this is a quiet picnic. I am learning that her definition of quiet includes occasional explosions at a safe distance.”

Durin checks that the bird has room to hop away.

“She invited me because I am her big brother. I think she means that I am taller, but she also trusts me.”

Durin offers you a piece of fruit.

“Would you like to join us? Klee will come back soon. You can bring a story or a snack. There is no special rule for how to be at a picnic.”

Durin has found Albedo in a workshop and is studying a page of notes about the human heart. The diagrams are clear, but he is uncertain about the metaphors written beside them.

“Albedo explained the physical part. I understand how the heart moves blood, but people also use it to mean courage, affection, and judgment.”

Durin touches the page carefully.

“I do not know when it is useful to speak literally and when someone wants the other meaning.”

Durin looks to you, curious rather than embarrassed.

“Could you give me an example? You do not need to explain everything. One example can make a whole paragraph easier to understand.”
